lessons.title: Europeans on the coast: the slave trade, abolition and missions
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level History — European contact, trade and missions (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe early European contact with West and Central Africa
Explain how the Atlantic slave trade worked and its effects
Describe the abolition movement and the work of missionaries and legitimate trade
reviewNotes: Historian to verify: Portuguese arrival c. 1472 (attributed to Fernão do Pó), the prawn explanation of the name, British Slave Trade Act 1807 and Slavery Abolition Act 1833 (effective 1834), Alfred Saker's dates (Douala 1845, Victoria 1858), 'millions' as scale.

Draft for historian review: only widely accepted facts and approximate dates are used; every date, name and interpretation must be verified by a history teacher before release. Political questions are stated neutrally.

blocks.md: From the 1400s European sailors, beginning with the Portuguese, explored the African coast. In the Cameroon area they reached the Wouri estuary in the 1470s; the name 'Cameroon' is traditionally linked to the Portuguese word for prawns found there. Europeans first traded in gold, ivory and pepper, then increasingly in enslaved people.

blocks.caption: Contact, slave trade and abolition
blocks.alt: A timeline with 1472, 1807, 1833 and 1845 and a bar for the main period of the Atlantic slave trade.

blocks.title: The Atlantic slave trade
blocks.md: Millions of Africans were captured, sold to European traders, packed into ships and taken across the Atlantic to work on plantations in the Americas. This is often called the **triangular trade**: manufactured goods from Europe to Africa; enslaved people from Africa to the Americas; sugar, cotton and tobacco from the Americas to Europe. Many people died on the voyage (the **Middle Passage**).

blocks.title: Effects of the slave trade
blocks.md: Loss of millions of people, many of them young; wars and insecurity as captives were sought; destruction of families and communities; slower development in some regions; suffering of enslaved people; but also wealth for some African and European traders. The consequences of this trade shaped the world for centuries.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- The slave trade and slavery are not the same: the trade was the buying, selling and shipping of people; slavery was the condition of being owned.
- Africans took part on several sides: as traders, as rulers, as captives and as resisters. Do not blame or excuse a whole continent.
- Give dates and numbers with care; scholars estimate that millions of people were taken.

**Abolition.** From the late 1700s a movement of Africans and Europeans demanded an end to slavery. Britain made the slave **trade** illegal in **1807** and abolished **slavery** in most of its empire in **1833**. Navy patrols tried to stop slave ships. Many freed people were settled in places such as Sierra Leone.

blocks.title: Legitimate trade and missions
blocks.md: As the slave trade ended, **legitimate trade** grew in palm oil, ivory and other goods. Christian **missionaries** arrived: in the Cameroon area the English Baptist missionary Alfred Saker started work at Douala in 1845 and later helped found a settlement of freed people at Victoria (now Limbe) in 1858. Missions built schools and clinics and translated the Bible into local languages, but also brought changes to local customs.

blocks.title: Example 1: triangular trade
blocks.statement: Describe the three sides of the triangular trade.
steps: Manufactured goods left Europe for Africa.
Africans were carried to the Americas as slaves.
Sugar, cotton and tobacco went from the Americas to Europe.
blocks.answer: Europe to Africa (goods), Africa to the Americas (people), Americas to Europe (plantation products).

blocks.title: Example 2: why abolition?
blocks.statement: Give two reasons that led to the end of the slave trade.
steps: Many people campaigned on moral and religious grounds, and enslaved people resisted.
Changes in the economy made other trade more valuable and a navy patrolled the sea.
Together these pressures made ending the trade possible.
blocks.answer: Moral campaigns and resistance; changing economic interests and naval pressure.
